content.paragraph: In this section we give geometric definitions of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas and derive their standard equations. They are called conic sections, or conics, because they result from intersecting a cone with a plane as shown in Figure 1.

The cones are arranged such that the first cone is upright with a horizontal base and the second cone is inverted and its tip touches the tip of the first cone and its base is parallel to the base of the first cone. subsection.title: Parabolas
subsection.paragraph: A parabola is the set of points in a plane that are equidistant from a fixed point $$F$$ (called the focus) and a fixed line (called the directrix). This definition is illustrated by Figure 2. Notice that the point halfway between the focus and the directrix lies on the parabola; it is called the vertex. The line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix is called the axis of the parabola.

figure.alt_text: Two lines, a parabola, and eight line segments are displayed. A dashed vertical line, labeled axis, is drawn perpendicular to a solid horizontal line, labeled directrix. The parabola opens upward and is symmetric about the axis. It crosses the axis at a certain distance above the directrix at a point labeled vertex. A point is marked above the vertex on the axis and labeled F. The point is also labeled focus. From F, a line segment slopes upward to the right until it reaches the right arm of the parabola. From this point, a vertical line segment descends downward to meet the horizontal line. The two-line segments are equal in length. From F, another line segment slopes downward to the right until it reaches the right arm of the parabola. From this point, a vertical line segment descends downward to meet the horizontal line. These two line segments are equal in length. Four more line segments are drawn similarly on the left side of the parabola.

subsection.paragraph: In the 16th century Galileo showed that the path of a projectile that is shot into the air at an angle to the ground is a parabola. Since then, parabolic shapes have been used in designing automobile headlights, reflecting telescopes, and suspension bridges. (See Problem 22 in Problems Plus following Chapter 3 for the reflection property of parabolas that makes them so useful.)

We obtain a particularly simple equation for a parabola if we place its vertex at the origin $$O$$ and its directrix parallel to the $$x$$-axis as in Figure 3. If the focus is the point $$(0,p)$$ , then the directrix has the equation $$y = - p$$ . If $$P(x,y)$$ is any point on the parabola, then the distance from $$P$$ to the focus is
and the distance from $$P$$ to the directrix is $$|y + p|$$ . (Figure 3 illustrates the case where $$p > 0$$ .) The defining property of a parabola is that these distances are equal:

subsection.paragraph: If we write $$a = 1/(4p)$$ , then the standard equation of a parabola (1) becomes $$y = ax^{2}$$ . It opens upward if $$p > 0$$ and downward if $$p < 0$$ [see Figure 4, parts (a) and (b)]. The graph is symmetric with respect to the $$y$$-axis because (1) is unchanged when $$x$$ is replaced by $$- x$$ .

subsection.title: Ellipses
subsection.paragraph: An ellipse is the set of points in a plane the sum of whose distances from two fixed points $$F_{1}$$ and $$F_{2}$$ is a constant (see Figure 6). These two fixed points are called the foci (plural of focus). One of Kepler’s laws is that the orbits of the planets in the solar system are ellipses with the sun at one focus.

Two points, located near the left and right sides of the ellipse are labeled F_1 and F_2, respectively. A line segment begins from F_1, slopes steeply upward to the right and meets the ellipse. The second line segment begins from this point, slopes down to the right, and reaches F_2. The third line segment begins from F_1, slopes gradually upward to the right and meets the ellipse at a point labeled P. The fourth line segment begins from P, slopes down to the right, and ends at F_2. The fifth line segment slopes downward the right to the right and meets the ellipse. The sixth line segment begins from this point, slopes upward to the left, and reaches F_2.

subsection.paragraph: From triangle $$F_{1}F_{2}P$$ in Figure 7 we can see that $$2c < 2a$$ , so $$c < a$$ and therefore $$a^{2} - c^{ 2} > 0$$ . For convenience, let $$b^{2} = a^{2} - c^{ 2}$$ . Then the equation of the ellipse becomes $$b^{2}x^{2} + a^{2}y^{2} = a^{2}b^{2}$$ or, if both sides are divided by $$a^{2}b^{2}$$ ,

Since $$b^{2} = a^{2} - c^{ 2} < a^{2}$$ , it follows that $$b < a$$ . The $$x$$-intercepts are found by setting $$y = 0$$ . Then $$x^{2}/a^{2} = 1$$ , or $$x^{2} = a^{2}$$ , so $$x = \pm a$$ . The corresponding points $$(a,0)$$ and $$( - a,0)$$ are called the vertices of the ellipse and the line segment joining the vertices is called the major axis. To find the $$y$$-intercepts we set $$x = 0$$ and obtain $$y^{2} = b^{2}$$ , so $$y = \pm b$$ . The line segment joining $$(0,b)$$ and $$(0, - b)$$ is the minor axis. Equation 3 is unchanged if $$x$$ is replaced by $$- x$$ or $$y$$ is replaced by $$- y$$ , so the ellipse is symmetric about both axes. Notice that if the foci coincide, then $$c = 0$$ , so $$a = b$$ and the ellipse becomes a circle with radius $$r = a = b$$ .

subsection.paragraph: Like parabolas, ellipses have an interesting reflection property that has practical consequences. If a source of light or sound is placed at one focus of a surface with elliptical cross-sections, then all the light or sound is reflected off the surface to the other focus (see Exercise 67). This principle is used in lithotripsy, a treatment for kidney stones. A reflector with elliptical cross-section is placed in such a way that the kidney stone is at one focus. High-intensity sound waves generated at the other focus are reflected to the stone and destroy it without damaging surrounding tissue. The patient is spared the trauma of surgery and recovers within a few days.

subsection.title: Hyperbolas
subsection.paragraph: A hyperbola is the set of all points in a plane the difference of whose distances from two fixed points $$F_{1}$$ and $$F_{2}$$ (the foci) is a constant. This definition is illustrated in Figure 11.

figure.caption: P is on the hyperbola when | PF 1 | - | PF 2 | = ± 2 a .
figure.alt_text: A hyperbola and two line segments are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The hyperbola resembles two parabolas that are mirror images of each other. The left part of the curve resembles the right angular bracket, with a rounded tip and arms slightly bulging outward. It has its vertex on the negative x-axis. A point is marked on the negative x-axis, to the left of the vertex, and is labeled F_1(negative c, 0). The right part of the curve resembles the left angular bracket, with a rounded tip and arms slightly bulging outward. It has its vertex on the positive x-axis. A point is marked on the positive x-axis, to the right of the vertex, and is labeled F_2(c, 0). From F_1(negative c, 0), a line segment slopes upward to the right, crosses the left part of the hyperbola, the y axis, and meets the upper arm of the right part of the hyperbola at a point labeled P(x, y). From P(x, y), a line segment slopes downward to the left and meets the positive x-axis at F_2(c, 0).

subsection.paragraph: Hyperbolas occur frequently as graphs of equations in chemistry, physics, biology, and economics (Boyle’s Law, Ohm’s Law, supply and demand curves). A particularly significant application of hyperbolas was found in the long-range navigation systems developed in World Wars I and II (see Exercise 53).

Notice that the definition of a hyperbola is similar to that of an ellipse; the only change is that the sum of distances has become a difference of distances. In fact, the derivation of the equation of a hyperbola is also similar to the one given earlier for an ellipse. It is left as Exercise 54 to show that when the foci are on the $$x$$-axis at $$( \pm c,0)$$ and the difference of distances is $$\left| \mathit{PF}_{1} \right| - \left| \mathit{PF}_{2} \right| = \pm 2a$$ , then the equation of the hyperbola is

where $$c^{ 2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$$ . Notice that the $$x$$-intercepts are again $$\pm a$$ and the points $$(a,0)$$ and $$( - a,0)$$ are the vertices of the hyperbola. But if we put $$x = 0$$ in Equation 6 we get $$y^{2} = - b^{2}$$ , which is impossible, so there is no $$y$$-intercept. The hyperbola is symmetric with respect to both axes.
To analyze the hyperbola further, we look at Equation 6 and obtain

This shows that $$x^{2} \geqslant a^{2}$$ , so $$|x| = \sqrt{x^{2}} \geqslant a$$ . Therefore we have $$x \geqslant a$$ or $$x \leqslant - a$$ . This means that the hyperbola consists of two parts, called its branches.

When we draw a hyperbola it is useful to first draw its asymptotes, which are the dashed lines $$y = (b/a)x$$ and $$y = - (b/a)x$$ shown in Figure 12. Both branches of the hyperbola approach the asymptotes; that is, they come arbitrarily close to the asymptotes. (See Exercise 4.5.77, where these lines are shown to be slant asymptotes.)

statement.paragraph: The LORAN (LOng RAnge Navigation) radio navigation system was widely used until the 1990s when it was superseded by the GPS system. In the LORAN system, two radio stations located at $$A$$ and $$B$$ transmit simultaneous signals to a ship or an aircraft located at $$P$$ . The onboard computer converts the time difference in receiving these signals into a distance difference $$\left| {PA} \right| - \left| {PB} \right|$$ , and this, according to the definition of a hyperbola, locates the ship or aircraft on one branch of a hyperbola (see the figure). Suppose that station B is located $$400$$ mi due east of station A on a coastline. A ship received the signal from station B $$1200$$ microseconds (μs) before it received the signal from station A.

item.paragraph: Assuming that radio signals travel at a speed of $$980{ft}/{\mu s}$$ , find an equation of the hyperbola on which the ship lies.
If the ship is due north of $$B$$ , how far off the coastline is the ship?

exercise_group.instructions: 67, 68, and 69 Reflection Properties of Conic Sections We saw the reflection property of parabolas in Problem 22 of Problems Plus following Chapter 3. Here we investigate the reflection properties of ellipses and hyperbolas.

statement.paragraph: Let $$P\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ be a point on the ellipse $$x^{2}/a^{2} + y^{2}/b^{2} = 1$$ with foci $$F_{1}$$ and $$F_{2}$$ and let $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ be the angles between the lines $$\mathit{PF}_{1}$$ , $$\mathit{PF}_{2}$$ and the ellipse as shown in the figure. Prove that $$\alpha = \beta$$ . This explains how whispering galleries and lithotripsy work. Sound coming from one focus is reflected and passes through the other focus. [Hint: Use the formula in Problem 21 in Problems Plus following Chapter 3 to show that $$\tan\alpha = \tan\beta$$ .]

figure.alt_text: An ellipse, two line segments, and a line are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The ellipse, labeled x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1, is symmetric about both the axes and its horizontal length is more than its vertical length. The left and right foci of the ellipse are on the x-axis at points labeled F_1 and F_2. From F_1, a line segment slopes upward to the right to meet the ellipse at a point labeled P(x_1, y_1) in the first quadrant. From this point, a line segment slopes downward to the right and meets the x-axis at F_2. A line is a tangent to the ellipse at P(x_1, y_1). The angle between F_1 P and the tangent is labeled alpha and the angle between F_2 P and the tangent is labeled Beta.

statement.paragraph: Let $$P\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ be a point on the hyperbola $$x^{2}/a^{2} - y^{2}/b^{2} = 1$$ with foci $$F_{1}$$ and $$F_{2}$$ and let $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ be the angles between the lines $$\mathit{PF}_{1}$$ , $$\mathit{PF}_{2}$$ and the hyperbola as shown in the figure. Prove that $$\alpha = \beta$$ . This shows that light aimed at a focus $$F_{2}$$ of a hyperbolic mirror is reflected toward the other focus $$F_{1}$$ .

figure.alt_text: The image has two parts. In the first part, a hyperbola, two line segments, and a line are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The branches of the hyperbola intercept the x-axis at their vertices. The left and right foci of the hyperbola are at F_1 and F_2, respectively. From F_1, a line segment slopes upward to the right to meet the upper arm of the right branch of the hyperbola at a point labeled P in the first quadrant. From P, a line segment slopes downward to meet the x-axis at F_2. A line enters from the bottom, slopes upward to the right, and is tangent to the hyperbola at P. The angle between F_1 P and the tangent is labeled alpha and the angle between F_2 P and the tangent is labeled Beta. In the second part of the figure, the same hyperbola as the first part, its tangent, and two line segments are shown. The left branch and the tangent are drawn with dashed and faded lines. The right branch is drawn with a solid line. A line segment enters from the top, slopes steeply down to the right, and meets the right branch at P. An arrow on the line segment points toward P. From P a second line segment slopes gradually down to the left until F_1. An arrow on this line segment points toward F_1. The first line segment extends further downward in a dashed line until it reaches F_2. The angle between the first line segment and the tangent, F_1 P and the tangent, and F_2 P and the tangent is equal.
